text: The mechanism of effect of support salt concentration in electrolyte on performance of lithium-sulfur cells E.V.
Kolosnitsyn Laboratory of Electrochemistry, Ufa Institute of Chemistry - Subdivision of the Ufa Federal Research Centre of the Russian Academy of Sciences, 69, Prosp.

Oktyabrya, Ufa, 450054, Russian Federation a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received 4 August 2018 Received in revised form 2 November 2018 Accepted 4 November 2018 Available online 9 November 2018 Keywords: Lithium-sulfur battery Concentration of support salt Solvation Sulfolane Cycling performance a b s t r a c t The effect of the lithium perchlorate concentration in sulfolane (in the range from 0.1M to 2.8М) on the performance of lithium-sulfur cells is studied.

It is shown that the concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane considerably affects the depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur, the reactivity of lithium polysulfides, and the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells.
The maximum depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur is reached at the concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane of 1.0M, while the minimum depth is reached at 2.8М.
The depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur is limited by the number of free solvent molecules.
An increase in the concentration of the support salt results in an increase in the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells.
At concentrations of the support salt above 2.4М, the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells is close to 100%.

We believe that the concentration of support salts affects the species of lithium polysulfides, their association-dissociation equilibria in electrolyte solutions and the processes of solvation of lithium ions contained in lithium polysulfides and support salts, and thus determines the performance of lithiumsulfur cells. © 2018 Elsevier Ltd.

Introduction Lithium-sulfur batteries are batteries with a liquid cathode, since the electroactive materials of the positive electrode (sulfur and intermediate products of its electrochemical reduction, lithium polysulfides) are soluble in the electrolyte [1e7].

The presence of active materials of the positive electrode in the liquid phase determines the considerable effect of the physicochemical properties of the electrolyte system on the regularities of chemical, physicochemical and electrochemical processes that occur in lithiumsulfur batteries during their charge, discharge and storage.

Ionic conductivity and viscosity are the most important properties of electrolyte systems as they affect the regularities of electrochemical transformations of the dissolved active materials (sulfur and lithium polysulfides).

The ionic conductivity and viscosity of the electrolyte systems are determined by many factors, the main ones being: the polarity and solvation properties of the solvents; the size, geometry and donor properties of anions in the support salts; and the concentration of the support salts in the electrolyte solutions.
The regularities of electrochemical transformations of sulfur and lithium polysulfides are determined by their species in the electrolyte solutions.
By chemical nature, lithium polysulfides (Li2Sn) are salts of polysulfane acids (H2Sn) [8].
Lithium polysulfides, dissolved in aprotic dipolar solvents, can undergo heterolytic (electrolytic) [9e11] (Equations (1) and (2)) and homolytic dissociation [12e22] (Equations (3) and (4)).

The heterolytic dissociation of lithium polysulfides, which can occur both by the first and second stages, produces charged particles (lithium cations and polysulfide anions): Li2Sn4Liþ þ LiSn (1) LiS n 4Liþ þ Sn2 (2) At electrolytic dissociation of lithium polysulfides e Li2Sn, the bond of Li-S breaks with the formation of lithium cations and mono- or dianions of polysulfides (Equations (1) and (2)).
The degree of electrolytic dissociation increases with increasing polarity and donor properties of solvents.

In the case of lithium polysulfides, the most stable radical is S3-, whose formation is shown in many works, for example [23].
Homolytic dissociation of Li2Sn can occur as in polar and as in low polar solvents [15,16,19].
Low polar solvents stabilize the lowordered lithium polysulfides, and the high polar ones stabilize the high-ordered lithium polysulfides and the anion radical S3-.
High polar and high donor solvents promote homolytic dissociation to form the radical anion S3-.

The radical species of lithium polysulfides, similarly to the molecular ones, can undergo electrolytic dissociation (Equation (5)): (5) As a result of the liability of lithium polysulfides to undergo heterolytic (electrolytic) and homolytic dissociation, electrolyte solutions generally simultaneously contain a lot of diverse molecular, radical, ion radical and ionic species of sulfur with various number of atoms that exist in dynamic equilibrium.
The species of lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions determine their reactivity.
Solutions of lithium polysulfides in aprotic dipolar solvents have high ionic conductivity that is comparable to that of readily ionizable lithium salts [24,25].
A specific feature of polysulfide solutions is that they have high viscosity, which is considerably higher than that of solutions of lithium salts with the same concentration.

For example, the 0.3m solution of Li2S6 in sulfolane has conductivity of 0.987 mS/cm and viscosity of 30 mPa s and 0.5m solution of LiClO4 in sulfolane has conductivity of 1.897 mS/cm and viscosity of 19 mPa s [26].
This indicates that lithium polysulfides form intermolecular associates in solutions [24e26].
The presence of support lithium salts in the electrolytes of lithium-sulfur cells affects the species of lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions and hence their reactivity.

In fact, in the presence of well ionizable salts (salts with high electrolytic dissociation constants), the electrolytic dissociation of lithium polysulfides will be suppressed to a considerable extent.

In support of arguments on suppression of electrolytic dissociation of lithium polysulfides, it is also possible to bring the fact that there is no synergetic effect in the specific conductivity of mixed solutions of lithium polysulfides and lithium perchlorate [26].
The degree of electrolytic dissociation of lithium polysulfides will also decrease in the presence of salts with low electrolytic dissociation constants but to a much smaller extent.

Furthermore, the support lithium salts, present in electrolytes, result in cationic linking of polysulfide anions [24], which impairs the transport properties of electrolyte systems and the segmental mobility of sulfur atoms in polysulfide chains.
The effect of lithium polysulfides on the properties of electrolyte solutions has been studied in a number of works [25e29].
It has been shown that the presence of lithium polysulfides affects the ionic conductivity of electrolyte solutions and increases their viscosity.

Even a brief consideration of the structure and properties of lithium polysulfide solutions in the electrolyte systems allows one to assume that the properties of lithium-sulfur batteries will largely depend on the nature and concentration of lithium salts in electrolytes.
For example, the effect of the concentration of lithium salts on the performance of lithium-sulfur cells was studied in a number of publications [6,30e39].

However, the published results of studies do not allow one to judge to the full extent about the mechanisms of the effect of the concentration of support salts on the processes into lithium-sulfur cells.

The purpose of this work is to clarify the mechanism by which the concentration of support salts in electrolytes affects the performance of lithium-sulfur cells, such as the depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur, the rate of capacity depletion and the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells. 2.
Objects studied and justification of their choice Electrochemical studies were performed in airtight stainless steel two-electrode disc cells by own design and production (Swagelok® cells).

The sulfur electrodes (d 1⁄4 2.85 cm, A 1⁄4 6.38 cm2) used in this study had the following composition: S (99.5%, Acros) - 70% wt., Ketjenblack EC-600JD (Akzo Nobel) - 10% wt., polyethylene oxide (ММ 1⁄4 4  106, Aldrich) - 20% wt.
The surface capacity of sulfur electrodes was 2 mAh/cm2, which is equivalent to the sulfur load about 1.2 mg/cm2.
The sulfur content in the positive electrodes (in mg of sulfur per cm2) was determined by thermogravimetry.
The theoretical capacity of the positive electrodes (in mAh per cm2) was calculated from the sulfur content in the electrodes.
The negative electrodes (d 1⁄4 2.55 cm, A 1⁄4 5.10 cm2) were made of lithium foil (99.9%, Russia) with a thickness of 120 mm.
The microporous polypropylene Celgard®3501 with a thickness of 25 mm (d 1⁄4 2.85 cm, A 1⁄4 6.38 cm2) was used as the separator.
Solutions of lithium perchlorate (LiClO4, 99.99% battery grade, Aldrich) in sulfolane (99.8%, GC, Sigma-Aldrich) were studied as the electrolyte solutions.
Lithium perchlorate is an effective polysulfide shuttle inhibitor [40].
Sulfolane is a solvent possessing high ionizing capability and well dissolving various lithium salts [41], including lithium polysulfides.
It should be noted that sulfolane has a high FlashPoint (>166 C [42]).
Gaseous products are not generated at the reaction of sulfolane with metallic lithium.
The concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane was 0.1М, 0.5М, 1.0М, 1.5М, 2.0М, 2.4М and 2.8М.
The content of electrolytes into lithiumsulfur cells was 4 ml per 1 mAh, which is equivalent to 6.7 ml per 1 mg of sulfur.
The electrolyte was introduced into lithium-sulfur cells using a “MICROLITERTMSyringe” (Hamilton Company, USA) with a volume of 50 ml.
The accuracy of electrolyte dosing into the cells was ±5%.
The ionic conductivity and viscosity of highly concentrated solutions of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane were measured using techniques similar to those presented previously [41].
All operations for the preparation of electrolyte solutions and assembling of lithium-sulfur cells were performed in a glove box in a dry air atmosphere (the water content did not exceed 10 ppm).
Galvanostatic charge and discharge cycling of lithium-sulfur cells were carried out using a BT-05PG battery tester in the voltage range of 1.5e2.8 V at þ 30 C.
The current density of the charge and discharge were 0.3 mA/cm2 (0.15C, 250 mA/g(S)).
The results of the electrochemical studies were processed using the Data Analyzer program, which is part of the specialized ElChemLab V1© software package.
The Data Analyzer program is E.V.

The program allows to process files with experimental data presented in a table containing information on the change in time of the current, the voltage on the cell, the potential of the working electrode vs. the reference electrode and other information (for example, data from external sensors).

The internal resistance of lithium-sulfur cells was calculated by Equation (6) at the specified depth of discharge: R 1⁄4 j Uch  Udch j=ðjichj þ jidchjÞ (6) where: R e internal resistance at the specified depth of discharge, Ohm$cm2; Uch e voltage on the cell at charge at the specified depth of the discharge, V; Udch e voltage on the cell at discharge at the specified depth of the discharge, V; jichj e module of current density of charging, A/cm2; jidchj emodule of current density of discharging, A/cm2.
To calculate the resistance value of lithium-sulfur cells at different charge states, a special calculation algorithm was developed, implemented in the ElChemLab V1© software package developed by us.

When developing the calculation algorithm, we studied the change in the self-discharge current depending on the degree of charge of lithium-sulfur cells and found that the selfdischarge current in the low voltage charge stage is substantially lower than at the high voltage stage.

When calculating the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells, the mean values of self-discharge currents at the low voltage and high voltage stages were calculated from the difference in the charge and discharge capacities at the low voltage and high voltage areas from the values of which the loss of the charging capacity was calculated for the low voltage and high voltage charging stages of lithium-sulfur cells.
For a unit of DoD (100% DoD), the experimentally obtained discharge capacity of lithium-sulfur cells was taken.
The correctness of this approach for calculating the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells was confirmed by independent impedance studies.

The self-discharge (shuttle) current density of lithium-sulfur cells was calculated by Equation (7): i 1⁄4 Q ch  Q dch ðtch þ tdchÞ$A (7) where: i e self-discharge (shuttle) current density, mA/cm2; Qch e total charge capacity at cycle, mAh; Qdch e total discharge capacity at cycle, mAh; tch e charging time, h; tdch e discharging time, h; A e active geometry area of electrodes, cm2. 3.

Effect of the concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane on the charge-discharge voltage profiles of lithium-sulfur cells Studies have shown that the concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane affects the charge-discharge voltage profiles of lithium-sulfur cells (Fig.1а).
The discharge voltage profiles of lithium-sulfur cells obtained in the first cycle contain two plateaus, irrespective of the lithium perchlorate concentration.
As an exception, the discharge voltage profiles of the cells with a highconcentration electrolyte containing 2.8М LiClO4 manifest only one high voltage plateau.

However, as lithium-sulfur cells with the high-concentrated electrolyte (2.8М LiClO4) are cycled, a low voltage plateau appears on the charge and discharge voltage profiles, and both the charge and discharge capacities increase (Fig. 1b and c).

As the concentration of lithium perchlorate in the electrolyte solution increases, the discharge capacity of lithium-sulfur cells first increases and then starts to decrease at salt concentrations in the electrolyte close to 1M (Fig. 2).
The decrease in the discharge capacity occurs due to a predominant capacity decrease on the second (low voltage) plateau.
As the lithium perchlorate concentration in the electrolyte increases, the voltages of the high voltage plateaus decrease, whereas those of the low voltage plateaus pass through a maximum (Fig. 3a).
At the high voltage plateau, there are two sections with different rates of capacity change.
The voltage of the high voltage stage was determined as the voltage in the middle of the first section of the high voltage plateau on the discharge curve, which usually corresponded to 100 mAh/g(S).

The voltage of the low voltage stage of the discharge was assumed to be equal to the value of the voltage at the maximum, which in most cases corresponded to the middle of the low voltage discharge plateau (Fig. 3b). 3.2.

Effect of the concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane on capacity depletion of lithium-sulfur cells during cycling The general regularities of charge and discharge capacity depletion of lithium-sulfur cells during cycling weakly depend on the support salt concentration, except for lithium-sulfur cells containing high-concentrated electrolytes (2.4М and 2.8М LiClO4) (Fig. 4).

At moderate support salt concentrations in the electrolyte (0.5e2.0М), the discharge capacity first quickly decreases during the cycling, then the capacity decrease slows down, and then the capacity starts to decrease abruptly again.

The shapes of the capacity depletion dependences of lithiumsulfur cells with high-concentration electrolytes on cycle number differ from similar dependences observed for lithium-sulfur cells with moderately concentrated electrolytes.
Of special interest is the dependence of capacity depletion of lithium-sulfur cells with the electrolyte containing 2.4М LiClO4 on cycle number.
The cells with the electrolyte containing 2.4М LiClO4 feature the smallest rate of depletion in both the charge and discharge capacities during cycling.

As lithium-sulfur cells with the high-concentration electrolyte (2.8М LiClO4) are cycled, the charge and discharge capacities increase and the maximum capacity values are reached by about the 40th cycle (Fig. 4).
After that, both the charge and discharge capacities start to decrease.

It should be noted that the dependences of capacity depletion on the number of charge-discharge cycles are functions of several parameters, such as the rate of destruction of electrolyte system components on the negative electrode, the passivation rate of the surface of carbon particles, the sulfur redistribution in the volume of the positive electrode in lithium-sulfur cells, etc.
The concentration of the support salt in the electrolyte affects the rates of all these processes but to a different degree.
Therefore, no strict and unambiguous correlations are observed between the shapes of the dependences of capacity depletion of lithium-sulfur cells during E.V.

cycling and the concentration of the support salt in the electrolyte.
At different stages of cycling, the rate of capacity depletion is determined by the action of various factors.
In the first-second cycles, the redistribution of sulfur over the volume of the lithiumsulfur cells has a significant contribution to the depletion in the capacity.
At the initial stages of cycling (first 10e30 cycles), the main contribution to the reduction in capacity is made by the displacement of sulfur onto the face of the sulfur electrode.
The resulting uneven distribution of sulfur over the volume of the sulfur electrode leads to a rapid decrease in the charge and discharge capacities of lithium-sulfur cells.

With subsequent cycling, the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells depletes mainly due to the simultaneous action of two factors - the decomposition of the electrolyte on the lithium electrode and the passivation of the surface of the carbon component of the sulfur electrode with poor soluble products of electrochemical reactions.
With a limited electrolyte content in lithium-sulfur cells after a certain number of cycles, the cell capacity decreases sharply to almost zero.
It should be mentioned that all of the factors listed above act simultaneously, but at different stages of the cycling, their contribution to the overall depletion in capacity is different. 3.3.

Effect of the concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane on the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells The coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells also depends on the support salt concentration and changes with cycling in a complex way (Fig. 5).
The lowest coulomb efficiency of cycling is observed for the cells with low concentrated electrolytes.
As the lithium perchlorate concentration increases, the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells increases.
The largest coulomb efficiency is observed for cells with high-concentration electrolytes containing 2.0e2.8М of the lithium salt.

Discussion Three aspects should be kept in mind in a consideration of the mechanisms of the effect of the concentration of support salts on the discharge capacity and cycling performance of lithium-sulfur cells:  species of lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions;  the association-dissociation equilibria in electrolyte solutions containing lithium salts and lithium polysulfides;  the processes of solvation of lithium ions contained in lithium polysulfides and support salts. 4.1.

Species of sulfur and lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions The electrochemical reduction of sulfur is a complex multistage process [43,44] involving electrochemical reactions, reactions of electrolytic and homolytic dissociation, and disproportionation of intermediate products of sulfur reduction - lithium polysulfides.
Species of sulfur are determined by the state of charge of lithium-sulfur cells.
Sulfur in the totally charged lithium-sulfur cell exists mostly in molecular forms.

Since elementary sulfur is prone to form molecules with various lengths and can exist in various crystallographic modifications, available experimental data hardly provide enough grounds for judging about the particular species of sulfur in charged lithium-sulfur cells after a number of charge- Fig. 2.

It can only be stated that sulfur in charged lithium-sulfur cells exists in solid state due to its poor solubility in the electrolyte.

However, it should also be kept in mind that even totally charged lithium-sulfur cells can contain a fraction of sulfur in high ordered lithium polysulfides dissolved in the electrolyte, as well as lithium sulfide.
The fraction of molecular species of sulfur in lithium-sulfur cells decreases with discharge, whereas the fraction of ionic species increases.
Ionic species of sulfur are lithium polysulfides with various lengths.
Lithium polysulfides do not exist in individual state but do exist as solvates with various compositions in solutions.
Solvate complexes of lithium polysulfides can be isolated in individual state.
When solvate complexes of lithium polysulfides are formed, solvent molecules are bound in solvate shells of lithium ions contained therein [45].
The species of lithium polysulfides in electrolytes are determined by the support salt concentration.
Due to the nature of the anions, it should be expected that the electrolytic dissociation constants of lithium polysulfides are considerably smaller than that of lithium perchlorate.

If this assumption is correct, the fraction of ionic species of lithium polysulfides in the electrolyte solution would decrease with the increase in the concentration of lithium perchlorate whereas the fraction of neutral species would increase.
In turn, the increase in the fraction of lithium polysulfides in neutral Fig. 4.

species would also result in the increase in the fraction of radical species of lithium polysulfides formed upon the homolytic dissociation of the former.
The species of lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions would affect their electrochemical activity.

It can be assumed that, due to the compensation of the negative charge on polysulfide anions by lithium ions, lithium polysulfides in neutral (molecular) and radical species would have the highest reactivity, whereas lithium polysulfides in ionic species would have the lowest reactivity.

We believe that compensation of the negative charge on the polysulfide chain will facilitate the transfer of the electron from the electrode to the polysulfide anion due to the decrease in the electrostatic interaction of the electron and the polysulfide anion. 4.2.

Association-dissociation equilibria of lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions A specific feature of lithium polysulfides is their liability to disproportionation reactions that result in lithium polysulfides with both smaller and larger amount of sulfur atoms in the polysulfide chain, as well as lithium sulfide.

The liability of lithium polysulfides to undergo disproportionation, electrolytic and homolytic dissociation results in the situation that the electrolyte solutions in lithium-sulfur cells simultaneously contain lithium polysulfides in various species: molecular, ionic, ion-radical and radical species.

The ability of lithium polysulfides to undergo disproportionation, electrolytic and homolytic dissociation affects the mechanisms of electrochemical processes that occur in lithium-sulfur cells during charge and discharge.

With consideration for the disproportionation and solvation of the resulting lithium polysulfides with solvent molecules, the scheme of electrochemical reduction of sulfur in lithium-sulfur cells can be presented as follows: High voltage stage (8) (9 and 10) (11) (12) (13) (14) (15) Low voltage stage 2Li2S4*2nSolv þ 4Liþ þ 4e/2Li2SY þ 2Li2S3*2nSolv (16) 2Li2S3*2nSolv4Li2S4*2nSolv þ Li2S2*2nSolv (17) Li2S4*2nSolv þ 2Liþ þ 2e/Li2SY þ Li2S3*2nSolv (18) Li2S3*2nSolv þ 2Liþ þ 2e/Li2SY þ Li2S2*2nSolv (19) 2Li2S2*2nSolv þ 4Liþ þ 4e/2Li2SY þ 4nSolv (20) n e the solvate number of lithium ion The scheme of reactions presented above is hypothetical.
However, the formation of polysulfide anions with various lengths and the S3- anion radical is confirmed by literature data [46].
This scheme does not include all reactions that can occur during the discharge of lithium-sulfur cells.

However, it clearly shows that the decrease in the order of polysulfides can occur both in disproportionation reactions (Equations (9), (10), (17)) and in electrochemical reactions (Equations (16), (18)e(20)).
Homolytic dissociation of lithium polysulfides (Equations (9), (10), (13)) can result in radical species of lithium polysulfides that possess high reactivity.
Binding of solvent molecules in solvate shells of lithium ions in lithium polysulfides occurs only upon the reduction of high-ordered lithium polysulfides (Equations (8), (12) and (15)).
Solvent molecules are released only upon reduction of lithium disulfide (Equation (20)).

The presence of long flat low voltage plateau on the discharge curve is explained by the fact that lithium trisulfide formed by electrochemical reduction of lithium tetrasulfide (Equation (16)) disproportionates to lithium tetrasulfide and lithium disulfide (Equation (17)).
Thus, lithium tetrasulfide predominantly electrochemically reduces on the low voltage stage.
Only at low concentrations of lithium polysulfides in solutions electrochemical reduction of lithium trisulfide (Equation (18)) and lithium disulfide (Equation (19)) begins.
The mechanism of the electrochemical reduction of short-chain lithium polysulfides is described in more detail in our works [43,45,47].
Our hypothetical scheme of electrochemical reduction of sulfur is in good agreement with the results of other studies.

The review [48] shows that the electrochemical reduction of sulfur involves complex and sequential equilibrium - reactions of electrochemical reduction of sulfur and lithium polysulfides and disproportionation and association with formation of anion and radical (mainly S3-) species of lithium polysulfides.
It is suggested that lithium sulfide (Li2S) can be formed both in electrochemical and chemical reactions.

On the surface of sulfur and lithium electrodes, various species of lithium polysulfides (di-anions, anions, radicals, and neutral species) and support salts participate in electrochemical and chemical reactions. 4.3.

Effect of solvation of lithium ions contained in lithium polysulfides and support salts on the discharge capacity of lithiumsulfur cells The electrochemical reduction of sulfur is accompanied by the formation of lithium polysulfides, compounds that are well soluble in electrolytes.

Dissolution of lithium polysulfides in the electrolyte solution results in binding of solvent molecules in solvate shells of lithium ions contained in lithium polysulfides (Equations (8), (12) and (15)).
As lithium-sulfur cells are discharged, the concentration of lithium polysulfides in electrolytes and hence the number of bound solvent molecules increase.
The increase in concentration of lithium polysulfides in the electrolyte solutions occurs until E.V.
Karaseva et al. / Electrochimica Acta 296 (2019) 1102e1114 1108
elementary sulfur is completely reduced to lithium tetrasulfide.
Electrochemical reduction of lithium tetrasulfide is not accompanied by the increase in the concentration of lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions (Equations (16) and (18)).
Therefore, its reduction does not change the concentrations of free and bound solvent molecules.
The increase in the concentration of lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions increases their viscosity and decreases the ionic conductivity [25].
During reduction, the mean molecular mass of lithium polysulfides decreases.
As a result, the viscosity of electrolyte solutions somewhat decreases and the ionic conductivity increases [49].

Furthermore, the mobility of lithium polysulfides increases due to two factors that act in the same direction, i.e., a decrease in their molecular mass and a decrease in the viscosity of electrolyte solutions.

Since solvent molecules are involved in the electrochemical reduction of sulfur and high-ordered lithium polysulfides, the depth of sulfur reduction is determined by the number of free solvent molecules, i.e., the solvent molecules not bound in solvate shells of lithium ions in the support salts.
To ensure complete sulfur reduction, enough free solvent molecules should be available for the solvation of lithium tetrasulfide.

Equations (8), (12) and (15) make it possible to calculate the number of solvent molecules required for the solvation of lithium tetrasulfide, as well as the molar ratio of sulfur and solvent ensuring complete reduction of sulfur.
Studies that we performed previously [45] have shown that the solvate number of lithium ion in lithium tetrasulfide in sulfolane solutions is 2.
In this case, the solvate number of lithium tetrasulfide is 4, while the molar ratio of the solvent to elementary sulfur is 1:1.

To estimate the possible depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur in the high voltage plateau, we performed calculations on the effect of average solvate number of lithium ion and support salt concentration on the number of free solvent molecules that can solvate the lithium ions in lithium tetrasulfide formed (Table 1, Equations S.1 & S.2 are given in Supplementary materials).

It follows from the calculations that electrochemical reduction of sulfur to lithium tetrasulfide in electrolytes with the lithium perchlorate concentrations studied and with the electrolyte content of 6.7 ml per 1 mg of S (4 ml per 1 mA h(S)) is only possible if the average solvate number of lithium ions is close to 2.
In other words, in the case of sulfolane, the minimum required value of solvate number is 2.
The calculation results are in good agreement with the experimental data.
In fact, as follows from Fig. 1, electrochemical reduction of sulfur to lithium tetrasulfide occurs even in electrolytes with high lithium perchlorate concentrations.
However, the reduction depth is limited by the number of free solvent molecules.
For example, at a salt concentration of 2.0M, the amount of free molecules of sulfolane in the electrolyte is 5.7M.
This amount of free sulfolane molecules is sufficient to fully solvate lithium ions in the system if the solvate number of the lithium ion is 2.
Sulfolane, due to the presence of two equivalent oxygen atoms, can act as a bidentate ligand, and one molecule of sulfolane can saturate two coordination sites in the solvation shell of lithium ion.
Table 1 summarized the value of calculated discharge capacity that can be reached at high voltage stage.
These results show is there enough amount of free molecules of solvent (in this case sulfolane) in the electrolyte to solvate the generated lithium tetrasulfide.

If the free solvent molecules are not sufficient to completely reduce the sulfur to lithium tetrasulfide, then on the discharge curves of lithium-sulfur cells, the capacity value obtained at the high voltage plateau, is less than the theoretical value of 418 mAh/g(S).

A comparison of the calculated and experimentally obtained discharge capacity of lithium-sulfur cells shows that the formation of lithium tetrasulfide is possible in all studied electrolyte solutions:  if the average solvate number of lithium ion is 2, the formation of lithium tetrasulfide is possible in all the electrolyte systems studied;  if the average solvate number of lithium ion is 3, the formation of lithium tetrasulfide is possible in electrolytes containing from 0.1M to 1.0M lithium perchlorate  if the average solvate number of lithium ion is 4, the formation of lithium tetrasulfide is possible in electrolytes containing from 0.1M to 0.5M lithium perchlorate. 4.4.

Effect of the support salt concentration on the depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur The depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur is determined by the reactivity of elementary sulfur and lithium polysulfides, on the one hand, and on the other hand, by the electrochemical reaction conditions e the transport properties of the electrolyte system, as well as the size and accessibility of the active surface of the carbon component in the sulfur electrode that plays the roles of the current collector and electron transfer mediator.

The dependence of the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells on the concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane is bell-shaped with a maximum at a salt concentration of about 1M (Fig. 2).
The isotherm of the specific ionic conductivity of lithium perchlorate solutions in sulfolane has a similar shape (Fig. 6).

The match of the positions of maxima on the concentration dependence of the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells and on the isotherm of lithium perchlorate solution conductivity indicates that the processes of ion transfer in the electrolyte solution and the depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur are controlled by the same factors - the mobility and concentration of lithium ions.

On the one hand, the increase in the support salt concentration increases the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte system, and on the other hand, it decreases the mobility of lithium polysulfides due to the increase in viscosity (Fig. 6).
We believe that the depth of the electrochemical reduction of lithium polysulfides is determined to a greater extent by the rate of charge transfer than by the transport properties of the medium.
The rate of charge transfer is controlled by the species of lithium polysulfides in electrolyte solutions, which depend on the concentration of the support salt.
Probably, that is why there is a correlation between the shape of isotherms of the conductivity and the depth of the electrochemical reduction of sulfur.

The rate of electrochemical reduction of high ordered lithium polysulfides is greater than the for low ordered lithium polysulfides indicated on the reactivity control of the electrochemical reduction of lithium polysulfides.
At the same time, the mobility of high ordered lithium polysulfides is less than the mobility of low ordered lithium polysulfides.

The rate of electrochemical reduction of lithium polysulfides with different order can be judged from the value of the internal resistance of lithium-sulfur cells at low and high depths of discharge, which is mainly determined by the resistance of charge transfer.

A low value of the internal resistance of lithium-sulfur cells at low discharge depths and a greater resistance at high discharge depths (Fig. 7a) indicate greater rate of reduction of sulfur and high ordered lithium polysulfides compared to the reduction rate of low ordered lithium polysulfides.
Of course, the mechanisms of electrochemical transformations of sulfur and lithium polysulfides in lithium-sulfur cells, especially with a limited electrolyte content, requires detailed study.
The assumption made by us is only a hypothesis and needs additional experimental confirmation.
The reactivity of various species of sulfur and lithium polysulfides decreases in the series: S > LiSn > Li2Sn > LiSn > Sn2.
The reactivity of sulfur and lithium polysulfides is determined by the electron density on the polysulfide chain.
In the case of elemental sulfur, all sulfur atoms are neutral, so elemental sulfur has the greatest reactivity.
In the radical species of sulfur LiSn, the negative charge on the polysulfide chain is compensated by the positive charge of the lithium cation.
Due to the peculiarities of the electronic structure, the radical species of lithium polysulfides have a greater reactivity than neutral ones, such as Li2Sn.
Ionic species of sulfur have a lower reactivity than neutral ones due to the presence of a negative charge on the polysulfide chain.
The higher the density of the negative charge, the lower the reactivity.

The decrease in the discharge voltage at the high voltage stage with the increase in the support salt concentration (Fig. 3) is apparently due to the suppression of the homolytic dissociation of high-ordered lithium polysulfides.
This results in the decrease in the concentration of neutral and radical species of lithium polysulfides that whose reactivity is higher than that of molecular species.

The increase in discharge voltage (Fig. 3) and the increase in the depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur at the low voltage stage (Fig. 2), which observed in the ascending region of the Qdisch. 1⁄4 f(Csalt) dependence, indicate that the increase in lithium perchlorate concentration in the electrolyte solution results in the increase in the reactivity of sulfur into low-ordered lithium polysulfides (n  4).

The increase in Li2Sn reactivity is apparently due to an equilibrium shift of electrolytic dissociation of lithium polysulfides (Equations (1) and (2)) towards the formation of molecular species of lithium polysulfides that possess higher reactivity than ionic species.

The subsequent decrease in the sulfur reduction depth in the descending region of the Qdisch. 1⁄4 f(Csalt) dependence can be explained by a considerable decline of the transport properties of the electrolyte system due to the increase in its viscosity (Fig. 6).
It is further decreased at high concentrations of lithium perchlorate (above 2М) by the shortage of free solvent molecules required for the solvation of lithium polysulfides.

The solvation energy of the lithium ion in electrolyte systems with different concentrations of lithium perchlorate practically does not change, therefore discharge voltage is determined to a greater degree by the kinetics of the electrode processes than by the thermodynamics of solvation of the lithium ion.

Similar studies were performed in electrolyte systems based on lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate (CF3SO3Li) and the nature of the anion of the support salt practically does not affect the general laws of electrode processes.

The values of the overvoltage at the electrodes and the resistance (conductivity) of the electrolyte during the discharge and charge of the lithium-sulfur cells change due to the dissolution of the generating lithium polysulfides in the electrolyte and the changes in their composition (the order of polysulfide).

The concentration of the support salt in the electrolyte affects its electrical conductivity and transport properties and species of lithium polysulfides in solutions, which in turn affects the electroconductivity of the electrolyte and the magnitude of the overvoltages on the positive and negative electrodes.

The magnitude of voltage changes on the discharge plateau indicates the degree of influence of the concentration of the support salt on the electrochemical processes on the electrodes of lithium-sulfur cells.
The stronger the influence, the lower the voltage. 4.5.

Effect of the support salt concentration on the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells The effect of the concentration of support salts on the reactivity of various species of sulfur and lithium polysulfides can be determined from the dependence of the DC resistance of lithium-sulfur cells vs. their depth of discharge.

The internal resistance of lithiumsulfur cells is composed of three constituents: the electrolyte resistance plus the charge transfer resistance on the positive and negative electrodes (Equation (22)): Rcell 1⁄4 Rel þ RLi þ RS (22) where: Rcell is the DC resistance of a lithium-sulfur cell, Ohm,cm2; Rel is resistance of the electrolyte solution, Ohm,cm2; RLi is the charge transfer resistance on the lithium electrode, Ohm,cm2; and RS is the charge transfer resistance on the sulfur electrode, Ohm,cm2.

The dependence of the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells on the depth of discharge is a curve with a complex shape where three regions corresponding to different discharge depths can be distinguished (Fig. 7a).
It is convenient to use the results of impedance studies [49] to analyze the contributions of various components to the total resistance of lithium-sulfur cells at various discharge depths.

As impedance studies have shown, at small discharge depths of 5e15% (1st region) the main contributions to the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells are made by the charge transfer resistance on the positive electrode in the electrochemical reduction of high-ordered lithium polysulfides (Li2Sn; n > 4) and by the resistance of passivating layers on the electrodes.

As high-ordered lithium polysulfides are reduced, the total concentration of lithium polysulfides in the electrolyte solutions increases, which considerably decreases the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte system.
Therefore, at depth of discharge of lithium-sulfur cells about 25e35%, the increase in their resistance is observed, with the main contribution coming from the resistance of the electrolyte solution.
This region corresponds to the complete reduction of elementary sulfur to soluble lithium polysulfides.
Therefore, the dependence of resistance on the depth of discharge passes through a maximum caused by the low electrolyte conductivity due to its saturation with lithium polysulfides.
Upon further discharge of lithium-sulfur cells, electrochemical reduction of lithium tetrasulfide and low-ordered lithium polysulfides occurs.

Since low-ordered lithium polysulfides possess higher mobility and affect the viscosity of the electrolyte system more weakly, the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte system increases, hence the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells decreases.

Therefore, the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells at depths of discharge of 60e80% is determined more considerably by the charge transfer resistance in the reduction of low-ordered lithium polysulfides (Li2Sn; n < 4) and the resistance of passivating layers on the sulfur electrode than by the electrolyte resistance and the charge transfer resistance on the lithium electrode.

Thus, the effect of the salt concentration on the reactivity of lithium polysulfides can be determined from the resistances in the minimum in the 1st and 3rd regions of the dependence of resistance on the depth of discharge of lithium-sulfur cells.

The observed dependences of the resistance of lithium-sulfur cells at various depths of discharge on the concentration of lithium perchlorate confirm the hypothesis on the increase in the content of molecular species of lithium polysulfides with the increase in the concentration of support salts and the higher electrochemical activity of molecular species in comparison with ionic species. 4.6.

Effect of the support salt concentration on the cycling performance of lithium-sulfur cells One of the most complex problems that needs to be resolved for creating commercially acceptable lithium-sulfur batteries is that their capacity fast decreases during charge-discharge cycling.

The decrease in the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells during cycling results from the simultaneous action of several factors, the main of which are listed below:  sulfur redistribution over the volume of lithium-sulfur cells;  sulfur transfer from the back-side space of the positive electrode to the front-side space;  sulfur encapsulation (as lithium sulfide) in the pore space of the carbon component;  passivation of the carbon component surface of the positive electrode;  decomposition of electrolyte system components (solvents and support salt anions).
The impact of these factors is determined by the concentration of the support salt.

As the support salt concentration increases, the rate of capacity depletion decreases, while the capacity of lithiumsulfur cells containing a high-concentrated solution increases rather than decreases in the initial stage of cycling.

One of the reasons of the decrease in the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells during cycling may lie in the passivation of the surface of carbon particles by hardly soluble products of electrochemical reactions - sulfur during the charge and lithium sulfide during the discharge.

If this hypothesis is correct, the decrease in the rate of capacity depletion of lithium-sulfur cells during cycling with the increase in the support salt concentration can be explained by hindrance of sulfur and lithium sulfide crystallization in high-concentrated electrolyte solutions. 4.7.

Effect of the support salt concentration on the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells The fact that the active material of the positive electrode of lithium-sulfur cells is located in electrolyte solutions results in a very undesirable phenomenon, i.e., direct reactions of sulfur and lithium polysulfides, dissolved in the electrolyte, with the metallic lithium electrode.
That decreases the coulomb efficiency of electrochemical processes in lithium-sulfur cells.
The rates of these reactions are determined by two factors: the transport properties of the electrolyte system and the transport properties of the surface electrolyte layer on the lithium electrode.

The composition and properties of the solid electrolyte on the lithium electrode surface and the transport properties of electrolyte systems are determined, to a considerable extent, by the concentration of the support salt.
As the support salt concentration in the electrolyte increases, the viscosity of the electrolyte system increases exponentially (Fig. 6).
Dissolution of lithium polysulfides in the electrolyte increases the viscosity of the electrolyte system even further.

Sulfur contained in molecular species of lithium polysulfides can be transferred only by diffusion, whereas sulfur within charged species (polysulfide anions) can be transferred both by diffusion and migration.
Since molecular species of lithium polysulfides are larger in size than ionic ones, the rate of sulfur transfer within lithium polysulfide molecules is lower than that within ionic particles.

Therefore, as the support salt concentration increases, the overall (diffusional and migrational) mobility of sulfur-containing particles decrease due to the increases in the viscosity of the electrolyte system.

Changes in the ionic composition of the electrolyte and in the mobility of sulfur-containing particles will also affect the composition of the surface film on the lithium electrode, and hence its transport properties.

It follows from the experimental data obtained (Fig. 5) that the coulomb efficiency quickly decreases at initial stages of lithiumsulfur cell cycling (5e10 cycles) in electrolyte solutions with low and moderate lithium perchlorate concentrations (0.5e1.5М) and then almost does not change.

In high-concentrated electrolyte solutions (with LiClO4 concentrations above 1.5M) the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells is higher than in less concentrated solutions and remains nearly unchanged during cycling.

High values of coulomb efficiency (more than 100%) in the high concentrated electrolyte (2.8M LiClO4) are explained by the fact that the experimentally determined discharge capacity of lithiumsulfur cells is greater than the charge capacity of the cells.

This is probably due to the fact that in high-concentrated electrolytes, because of their high viscosity, only a part of sulfur in the positive electrode is partly electrochemically reduced at the first cycles.
During cycling, the part of sulfur electrochemically reduced increases, which leads to the increase in the discharge capacity of lithium-sulfur cells and the decrease in coulomb efficiency.

The decrease in coulomb efficiency at initial stages of cycling in electrolytes with low and moderate concentrations of lithium perchlorate can be due either to improvement of the transport properties of the surface film on the lithium electrode or to a growth of the lithium electrode surface due to dispersion of metallic lithium.
It is possible that both factors act simultaneously.
Identification of the reasons of the decrease in the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells requires additional experimental studies.

The increase in the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithiumsulfur cells with the increase in concentration of support salt is most likely due to the slowness of interelectrode sulfur transfer due to the increase in the viscosity of electrolyte solutions [50].

The decrease in the self-discharge (shuttle) current density of lithium-sulfur cells with the increase in the viscosity of solutions of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane (Fig. 5b) may indicate that the increase in the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells with the increase in the concentration of the support salt is mainly due to the delay in interelectrode transfer of sulfur and lithium polysulfides. 5.

Conclusions The concentration of lithium salts in electrolyte solutions (lithium perchlorate in sulfolane) has a considerable effect on the properties and regularities of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells.
As the concentration of the support salt increases, the discharge capacity of lithium-sulfur cells first increases, then decreases.
The increase in the discharge capacity mainly occurs due to the increase in the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells at the low voltage stage.
The maximum discharge capacity of lithium-sulfur cells is reached at E.V.

lithium perchlorate concentration in sulfolane equal to 1М.
The dependence of the discharge capacity of lithium-sulfur cells on the support salt concentration well correlates with the ionic conductivity isotherm of LiClO4 solutions in sulfolane.
The depth of electrochemical reduction of sulfur is limited by the number of free solvent molecules.

As the concentration of lithium perchlorate in sulfolane increases, the reactivity of high-ordered lithium polysulfides decreases, while that of low-ordered ones first increases but starts to decrease at LiClO4 concentrations above 1.5М.
The capacity of lithium-sulfur cells changes in a complex way during cycling, depending on the support salt concentration.
The smallest change in the capacity of lithium-sulfur cells during cycling is observed at 2.4M concentration of the support salt in the electrolyte.
The increase in the concentration of the support salt results in the increase in the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells.
At concentrations of the support salt above 2.4М, the coulomb efficiency of cycling of lithium-sulfur cells is close to 100%.

We believe that the concentration of support salts affects the species of lithium polysulfides, their association-dissociation equilibria in electrolyte solutions and the processes of solvation of lithium ions contained in lithium polysulfides and support salts, and thus determines the performance of lithium-sulfur cells.
